column4: The source glosses maʿīn as flowing water and says the surah’s opening question turns toward it; here the Prophet is told to ask who could restore water if it sinks away, locating the stream beyond the blocker’s control.

The source’s maʿīn is flowing water; this verse joins it to qarār, a settled place, in God’s shelter for Mary and her son, matching the section’s water-bearing refuge and abundant pasture where animals can stay.
The source explicitly extends the dictionary form ṭaʿām to water; in Ṭālūt’s river test, whoever does not yaṭʿamhu (taste/drink it) is not of his company, so the verse makes that extension concrete.

Rain is drink and brings forth vegetation where livestock graze (فِيهِ تُسِيمُونَ); this directly joins water to pasture, as the section’s explanation of how water feeds the ground and keeps animals there does.
This verse says the water produces crops and fruit; 16:10 names the same rain, drink, and grazing vegetation, completing the section’s route from water to growth and provision.
The verse puts earth’s paths, rainwater, and varied plants in one scene; the source’s waterbeds in valleys and the water that makes pasture grow meet this same route through land.
The source describes pasture that lets animals remain; this verse says to eat and graze livestock (كُلُوا وَارْعَوْا أَنْعَامَكُمْ), following 20:53’s rain and plant growth.
The source’s secondary gloss for miskin invokes pasture, and 79:31 names both water and pasture (مَاءَهَا وَمَرْعَاهَا) as what is brought from the earth.

The source traces water into pasture for animals; this verse calls the preceding provision enjoyment for people and livestock (لَكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ), continuing 79:31’s water and pasture across 79:32.

The source names the channels of water in a valley; here water runs through valleys (فَسَالَتْ أَوْدِيَةٌ بِقَدَرِهَا), and the verse’s foam-versus-benefit parable makes the useful flow distinct from what passes.

The section says flowing water reaches soil and grows pasture; this verse describes water channeled as springs through earth and crops, then those crops yellow and become debris, setting growth beside its loss.
Water is driven to barren land, crops are brought out for people and their livestock; this directly stages the section’s water-to-soil-to-animal provision.
The source describes water nourishing land and pasture; this verse says the water revives a dead town and waters livestock and people, while 25:48 names the water sent down.
The source says the water is not something the blocker made; here God sends it in measure, settles it in the earth (فَأَسْكَنَّاهُ), and can take it away, making control of the supply the boundary.

The source insists the flowing water does not originate in the withholding hand; this verse asks whether people sent drinking water down from the clouds or God did (أَأَنْتُمْ أَنْزَلْتُمُوهُ مِنَ الْمُزْنِ أَمْ نَحْنُ الْمُنْزِلُونَ).
The section says the Quran turns an “Have you seen?” question toward water; this verse asks whether the hearers have considered the water they drink, and 56:69 names its divine source.

The section’s flowing supply can be obstructed, yet was not produced by the person who withholds it; the garden owner’s water becomes غَوْرًا and cannot be reached, a direct boundary on human control.
The section’s hand can block a watercourse but cannot determine its source; this continuation says God could make drinking water bitter (أُجَاجًا), showing a further limit on human control.
The source treats water as provision that reaches the land; this verse calls the sent-down water pure, and 25:49 completes the scene with dead land revived and livestock watered.
The source’s central claim is that a person holds back water they did not originate; here God sends water that grows beautiful gardens and asks who else could do this.

This repeats the source’s wording from 107:3, «ولا يحض على طعام المسكين»; 69:33 gives the surrounding claim about not believing in God, so this row isolates the same failure to urge food for the poor.
This says people do not urge one another to feed the poor (وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ), extending the same negative feeding scene from 107:3 to a communal relation.
The source quotes the root form مَنَّاعٌ لِلْخَيْرِ for one who keeps goodness back; this ayah uses that same wording for a character who hinders good.
The source’s secondary gloss develops pasture; this verse names pasture itself (الْمَرْعَىٰ) as what God brings forth, a direct verbal and field-image match.
The source glosses maʿīn as flowing water; this paradise scene serves a cup from maʿīn (كَأْسٍ مِّن مَّعِينٍ), using the named word in another setting.
The source glosses maʿīn as flowing water; this paradise passage also names cups from maʿīn (كَأْسٍ مِّن مَّعِينٍ), carrying the word into a different drinking scene.
The source’s stream is a resource someone can block; here God’s servants drink from a spring that they make gush forth (عَيْنًا يَشْرَبُ بِهَا عِبَادُ اللَّهِ), followed in 76:8 by feeding the needy.
Where the source’s figure withholds water and does not urge food for the needy, this passage feeds food to a poor person, an orphan, and a captive; 76:6 has just pictured a spring for God’s servants.

The source explicitly says the sheltering verb in 23:50 is the same as the orphan’s shelter here (فَآوَىٰ); this brings the section’s water-bearing refuge into relation to God’s shelter of a vulnerable child.

The source’s dictionary gloss for miskin describes a pasture so ample there is no need to leave for ظعن; this verse names dwellings and animal-fiber goods usable on a day of travel or a day of staying, giving that movement/staying contrast a concrete scene.

The source’s failure is not urging food for the miskin; these garden owners deliberately plan that no poor person enter before the harvest (أَن لَّا يَدْخُلَنَّهَا الْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكُم مِّسْكِينٌ), a direct denial of provision.
The section shows a person blocking a watercourse; in Salih’s people’s test, water is explicitly a share between them (الْمَاءُ قِسْمَةٌ بَيْنَهُمْ), with a turn for each drinker.

The source depicts water being kept back from others; here the she-camel and the people each have an allotted drinking day (لَهَا شِرْبٌ وَلَكُمْ شِرْبُ يَوْمٍ مَّعْلُومٍ), a specific counter-scene of shared water.
Against the section’s blocked watercourse, God brings twelve springs from the rock and tells the tribes to eat and drink from His provision (كُلُوا وَاشْرَبُوا مِن رِّزْقِ اللَّهِ).
This retelling likewise gives the tribes twelve springs from a rock and tells them to eat and drink from God’s provision; it repeats the shared-water scene that contrasts with withholding.
The section links a water source to animals and their sustenance; at Midian’s watering place, shepherds water their flocks while two women wait back, making access to water for herds the scene.
The section’s figure impedes a resource; Moses instead draws water for the two women’s flock (فَسَقَىٰ لَهُمَا), a specific act of supplying water to people waiting at the well.

The source’s withholding hand does not own the water it blocks; after the feeding scene in 76:8, this verse says the givers seek only God’s countenance and no reward or thanks, completing the opposing motive.

The source’s dictionary gloss for miskin connects staying to abundance; this verse describes a secure, tranquil town receiving provision abundantly, then losing that ease to hunger after denying God’s favors, a specific reversal of settled provision.

The source follows water into productive ground; this garden scene says both gardens yielded their fruit and a river was made to flow between them (وَفَجَّرْنَا خِلَالَهُمَا نَهَرًا), joining water and yield.
The source traces water into pasture and provision; this passage starts by describing rain poured down (صَبَبْنَا الْمَاءَ صَبًّا), then names fruit and fodder at 80:31 and recipients at 80:32.
The source’s water grows pasture; this verse names fruit and fodder (فَاكِهَةً وَأَبًّا), with 80:25 giving the rain at the start and 80:32 naming people and livestock as recipients.

The source describes pasture sustaining animals; this verse says the preceding food and fodder are provision for people and livestock (لَكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ), continuing the rain-and-growth scene begun at 80:25.
The source describes pasture as plentiful enough for animals to stay; this neighboring verse turns the pasture of 87:4 into dark debris (غُثَاءً أَحْوَىٰ), giving the growth a specific reversal.
The source’s 107:3 image is food urged for the poor; this verse names feeding on a day of hunger (إِطْعَامٌ فِي يَوْمٍ ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ) as one concrete response to deprivation.
The source names the miskin who is not urged food; this passage specifies a needy person in dust (مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ) as a recipient, while 90:14 names feeding during hunger.

The section connects ample pasture with no need to migrate away; here hypocrites explicitly urge that spending stop until the people around the Messenger disperse (لَا تُنفِقُوا عَلَىٰ مَنْ عِندَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ حَتَّىٰ يَنفَضُّوا), a specific reversal in which provision is withheld to force departure.
The section traces water into growth on the ground; this verse repeats that sequence as water from the sky brings out varied plants, grain, and fruit.
The section’s water reaches ground and enables growth; here a heavy cloud is driven to dead land, rain is sent, and fruit is brought forth, a specific rain-to-yield scene.
This verse joins water sent from the sky, fruit provided to people, and rivers made serviceable; it gives another concrete scene of water and provision that matches the section’s flow-to-growth path.
The section connects water with the growth that feeds living things; this verse says rain brings fruits as provision on the earth made as a dwelling place.
The section says water reaches soil and makes pasture grow; this verse describes land swelling and producing every kind of lovely growth after rain.
The section’s dictionary pasture is abundant enough to keep animals in place; this verse’s water-grown vegetation becomes scattered dry debris, a specific reversal of that lush field image.

The source says the water-holder did not originate the supply; this verse describes rain-grown vegetation, then a land whose owners think they control it before it is cut down, exposing that claim’s limit.
This is an interpretive extension of the section’s abundant pasture image: here rain-grown vegetation first pleases its cultivators, then yellows and becomes debris, showing how such growth can pass.
The section follows water into pasture and provision; this verse describes blessed rain producing gardens and grain, another specific water-to-crop scene.
This verse calls the preceding rain-grown yield provision for servants and says it revives dead land; 50:9 supplies the water, gardens, and grain at the start of the passage.
The section connects water to food-bearing ground; this verse describes dead earth made alive and grain brought out for people to eat, while 36:34 continues with gardens and springs.
This verse joins gardens to springs made to gush forth (وَفَجَّرْنَا فِيهَا مِنَ الْعُيُونِ), a direct image of water flowing into productive ground; 36:33 names the grain from that land.
The section extends feeding to water; this verse turns the preceding garden-and-spring scene into fruit for eating, following 36:34’s springs and gardens.
The section traces water to pasture growth; this adjacent passage asks what people cultivate, then 56:64 asks who actually makes it grow, before 56:68 turns to drinking water.
The source says the withholding person did not make the water; this verse asks whether people or God make the crop grow, just before 56:68–69 asks who sends down drinking water.
The section describes the pasture’s life-giving growth; this verse says God could turn the crop to dry debris, and the following 56:68–70 makes water’s source and vulnerability explicit.
The section describes water reaching soil and producing growth; this verse says earth that looks lifeless stirs and swells when water is sent down, and attributes that revival to God.
The section condemns failing to urge food for the poor; this verse tells people to eat the crop’s fruit and give its due on harvest day, a concrete rule for sharing field produce.

The source says a person withholds water that was not made by his hand; this verse condemns miserliness, urging others to be miserly, and concealing God’s bounty, a specific parallel in how received provision is kept back.
This verse repeats the pattern of miserliness and hiding what God has bestowed; it matches the section’s claim that the withheld water is not the withholder’s creation.

The source explicitly names the root m-n-ʿ for preventing good and pictures a blocked watercourse; this verse uses the same root for barring people from God’s mosques, extending that act of obstructing access to a shared good.

The section pictures a hand stopping water and withholding help; this verse describes hypocrites as physically withholding their hands and forbidding good, a specific parallel in the act of keeping aid back.
This verse introduces the she-camel as the test for Salih’s people; 54:28 then gives the specific water-sharing arrangement between them and the camel.
After 54:28 assigns shares of water, this verse says the people called their companion, who hamstrung the she-camel, completing the passage’s reversal of the shared-water arrangement.
This verse names paths made through the earth (سُبُلًا); 43:11 continues with water sent down in measure and land revived, recalling the section’s watercourses through valleys.

This verse describes measured rain reviving a dead town; 43:10 immediately before it names the paths through the earth, together giving a specific land-and-water scene parallel to the section’s channels.
The section names valley watercourses; this verse asks who placed rivers through the earth and set barriers between bodies of water, continuing the creation-and-water scene of 27:60.
